content: The 2016 Global Status Report on Blood Safety and Availability, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017, provides a comprehensive analysis of the global state of blood safety and availability. This report is based on data collected from 156 of the 195 WHO Member States, representing 93% of the global population. The data primarily reflects the year 2013 and was gathered through the WHO Global Database on Blood Safety (GDBS), which was established in 1998 to address concerns about the availability, safety, and accessibility of blood for transfusion. The report highlights the critical role of blood as a healthcare resource, essential for a wide range of clinical services. In high-income countries, blood transfusions are most commonly used in cardiovascular and transplant surgeries, trauma care, and cancer therapies. In contrast, in low-income countries, blood transfusions are more frequently used to manage pregnancy-related complications and severe childhood anemia. Ensuring a sufficient and safe blood supply is a fundamental component of a robust health system and is vital for achieving universal health coverage. However, the report underscores significant disparities in blood availability and safety across regions and income groups. For example, while high-income countries collect a substantial proportion of their blood supply from voluntary, non-remunerated donors, low-income countries often rely heavily on family/replacement and paid donors. This reliance increases the risk of transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs) such as HIV and hepatitis, which remain a major public health concern. The report also emphasizes the importance of effective surveillance and vigilance systems to monitor and improve blood safety. New and emerging pathogens pose additional threats to the blood supply, further highlighting the need for coordinated national and global efforts. The WHO has been conducting biennial surveys on blood safety and availability since 1998, and since 2006, data collection has been standardized and conducted annually. Key findings from the report include: 1. Global Blood Donations: In 2013, approximately 112.5 million blood donations were reported worldwide, with 89% collected as whole blood and 11% through apheresis procedures. The availability of blood for transfusion varies significantly across WHO regions and income groups. For instance, the European Region, which accounts for only 11% of the global population, reported 30% of global blood donations. In contrast, the African Region, home to 13% of the global population, accounted for only 4% of global donations. 2. Voluntary Non-Remunerated Donations: Seventy-four countries reported collecting more than 90% of their blood supply from voluntary, non-remunerated donors. However, 71 countries remain heavily dependent on family/replacement and paid donors, with these donations accounting for more than 50% of their blood supply. High-income countries reported the highest proportion of voluntary, non-remunerated donations (95%), compared to 63% in low-income countries. 3. Blood Safety: The prevalence of TTIs in donated blood remains a concern, particularly in low-resource settings. 4. Blood Component Processing: The processing of whole blood donations into components varies widely across regions. High-income countries are more likely to separate whole blood into components such as red cells, platelets, and plasma, optimizing its clinical use. 5. Discarded Blood: A significant proportion of blood donations are discarded due to reactivity for TTI markers, expiry, or other reasons. The percentage of discarded donations is higher in low-income countries, reflecting challenges in quality assurance and inventory management. 6. Governance and Funding: The report stresses the importance of nationally coordinated blood transfusion services, governed by quality management systems and supported by sufficient and sustainable funding. Integration of these services into national health systems is essential for ensuring timely access to safe and sufficient blood supplies. The report concludes that while progress has been made in improving blood safety and availability, significant challenges remain, particularly in low-resource settings. The ultimate goal is to leave no country behind in achieving universal health coverage and securing a safe and sufficient blood supply for all.
